new_en: [8] [Levush] "One does not recite Shehecheyanu," etc. Abudraham explains that from Pesach until Shavuot the world is in distress concerning the grain and the trees. God therefore commanded us to count these days so that we remember that distress, return to Him wholeheartedly, and plead before Him to have mercy upon the grain. Another reason for the counting is that each member of Israel is occupied during the harvest season, and He therefore commanded them to count so that they would know when Shavuot arrives. They also alluded through this to the seventh millennium, which is entirely Shabbos. Therefore there is an Atzeret on the seventh day of Pesach, Shavuot comes after 7 weeks, and the eighth day of Sukkot alludes toward the World-to-Come and to the great Jubilee. Rabbeinu Yerucham. In Tzeidah LaDerech I found that the ancients treated the 7 planets as deities. Bilam therefore offered 7 altars, and each of the 7 has 7 forms of dominion, totaling 49. The Torah therefore commanded the counting and gave the Torah on the 50th day, commanding that they not be worshiped. At Matan Torah God tore open the 7 heavens and opened the 7 earths so that all would know that there is no God besides Him.

"Rejoicing." It is written in the Kavanos that a certain great person was accustomed to recite Nachem every day, and he recited it also on Lag BaOmer and was punished. See there.

"Tachanun." This applies also on the evening of the 32nd day. In Ashkenaz the custom is that Tachanun is not said at Shacharit, whereas in the evening it is said. Accordingly, what Rama writes, that one may not take a haircut until Lag BaOmer itself, follows the Ashkenazic custom. Those whose custom is not to say Tachanun from the preceding evening may likewise take a haircut then, since the 2 matters depend upon one another. Mateh Yosef writes likewise. Chok Yaakov.

"Shabbos." This is the view of Mahari Weil. Maharil prohibits, and so do some later authorities. Nevertheless, where the established custom is permissive, that custom may be followed and one should not be stringent in these laws, as stated in seif katan 3. Chok Yaakov.

"Brit milah." See Beit Yosef, siman 559, where it is explained that the baalei brit are the sandakim, the mohel, and the father of the infant receiving brit milah, even if he does not perform the brit milah himself. They may take a haircut on the preceding evening before entering the synagogue. So state Minhagim, Chok Yaakov, and Peri Chadash, unlike Shiyarei Knesset HaGedolah. This is the custom.

"And one increases somewhat in rejoicing." Magen Avraham writes that a certain great person was accustomed to recite Nachem throughout the days of the Omer, recited it on Lag BaOmer, and was punished.

"And one does not say Tachanun on it." This applies also on the evening of the 32nd day. Minhagim writes in the laws of Tachanun that this is the custom in Moravia and Bohemia. Maharil, however, writes that the custom in Ashkenaz is not to say Tachanun at Shacharit, while in the evening Tachanun is said. Accordingly, Rama's statement that one does not take a haircut until Lag BaOmer itself follows Maharil according to his custom. Those whose custom is not to say Tachanun from the preceding evening may likewise take a haircut from then, because the 2 matters depend upon one another. Mateh Yosef writes similarly.

"They have the custom to take a haircut on Friday." Meaning for the honor of Shabbos. This is the view of Mahari Weil. Maharil prohibits, and some later authorities agree. Nevertheless, where the established custom is permissive, it may be followed, and one should not impose additional stringency in these laws.

"And one who is a baal brit." The baalei brit are the sandak, the mohel, and the father of the infant receiving brit milah, even if the father is not the mohel. They may take a haircut on the preceding evening before entering the synagogue, as stated in Minhagim and by the later authorities.

(6) "Until Lag BaOmer." This is inclusive, meaning through 33 complete days, each with its night and day. On the 34th day they were stringent only during the night; once daylight appears after sunrise it is permitted because part of a day is considered like the entire day.

(7) "For they say that then they ceased," etc. Although students also died on the 34th day, and for that reason they were stringent throughout the night of the 34th until sunrise, it is possible that the principal cessation was on the 33rd day and only a few died on the 34th. [Pri Megadim]

(8) "On the 33rd day." This view holds that the deaths ceased entirely on Lag BaOmer.

(9) "And one does not say Tachanun on it." This applies also on the preceding evening, the evening following the 32nd day.

(10) "Until Lag BaOmer itself." Meaning after sunrise, because part of the day is considered like the entire day.

(11) "And not from the evening." Some later authorities are lenient to permit haircuts from the preceding evening. Nevertheless, the later authorities conclude that regarding marriage no leniency was commonly practiced until Lag BaOmer by day, not on the preceding night. If Lag BaOmer falls on Friday and he is under pressure to make the necessary preparations by day, there may be room to be lenient from the preceding night.

(12) "A baal brit." Meaning the sandak, the mohel, and the father of the infant receiving brit milah, even if the father is not himself the mohel. What Rama writes concerning "the brit milah of his son" means that his son is receiving brit milah. The attendants who bring the infant in and out are not included.

"From 'In the third month.'" See Mishnah Berurah; I will explain somewhat. There are 2 systems of cantillation for the Aseret HaDibrot, commonly called the upper and lower cantillation. Their difference follows 2 distinct ways of dividing the text into verses.

The first system is arranged according to the written parashiyot, so that each dibbur is treated as its own unit. From Anochi through Lo Tisa is written as 1 closed parashah and constitutes 1 dibbur, and therefore is read as 1 verse. Likewise, from Zachor through Lo Tirtzach is treated as the unit of that dibbur. From Lo Tirtzach through Lo Tachmod, however, the text is written as 4 separate closed parashiyot, corresponding to 4 separate dibrot, and therefore each is treated as a separate verse. The cantillation and pronunciation accordingly reflect where the verse endings fall. Letters that receive dagesh or become soft, and vowels that vary because of a sof pasuk, follow that division.

The second system is arranged according to the ordinary reading division of the verses. In that reading, Lo Tirtzach through Lo Tachmod forms a single verse and one may not make a complete stop in its middle, even when reading privately. It cannot be said that Lo Tirtzach alone forms an independent verse, because there is no verse in the Torah containing fewer than 3 words. By contrast, the passages from Anochi through Lo Tisa and from Zachor through Lo Tirtzach are divided into several verses in the ordinary reading. Therefore the lower cantillation both joins the clauses that belong to 1 ordinary verse and separates the places where the ordinary reading has verse endings.

This is the substance of the 2 melodies. On Shavuot the custom is to use the upper cantillation, treating each dibbur as a distinct verse in accordance with the manner in which the Aseret HaDibrot were given. In Parashat Yitro and Parashat Vaetchanan during the regular yearly reading, the common custom is to use the lower cantillation. Some communities, however, are accustomed to use the upper cantillation also there when reading publicly, while an individual reading for himself uses the lower cantillation.

The practical pronunciation of the several words that change according to pause or continuation follows whichever cantillation is being used. Thus where a word concludes a verse in 1 system it receives the pronunciation appropriate to a stop, while in the other system it is pronounced as a continuing word. This is the general explanation of the 2 systems.

"Rather, she sets it aside until evening and burns it." The Mishnah states that she sets it aside until evening and then burns it. Gra already notes the difficulty, because the accepted rule is that consecrated items are not burned at night. The case appears to concern challah or terumah that became definitely impure, as is evident from the sugya in Bameh Madlikin and from the related Talmudic discussions.

The early authorities already addressed this wording. Ramban, Rashba, Ritva, Ran, and Maharam Chalava cite the Yerushalmi and discuss whether the phrase should be understood literally, whether this burning differs from the ordinary burning of sacred items, or whether the text reflects an opinion in the Yerushalmi that permits such burning at night. We do not generally rule in accordance with an opinion that allows burning sacred items at night. The wording of the Mishnah therefore requires interpretation in light of the explanations of those Rishonim. See their discussions in the cited passages.

(21) "Mugmar." Fumigation with incense is not something equally enjoyed by all people, but principally by those accustomed to luxuries, and was therefore not permitted on Yom Tov. Regarding smoking tobacco on Yom Tov, see Biur Halacha.

(22) "Upon the coals." With wood coals this is forbidden even if they were originally kindled for food preparation, because placing the spices on them initially somewhat extinguishes the coals and afterward kindles the spices. All the more so is it forbidden if he kindled the coals specifically for this purpose. The Gemara implies that even a pottery coal, meaning a piece of pottery heated for roasting meat upon it, is forbidden.

(23) "To fumigate the house." This is forbidden specifically when one performs the fumigation on Yom Tov. Before Yom Tov, however, one may take an iron vessel full of holes, fumigate it with spices, and plug the holes; on the following day he may open the holes and the house will then be perfumed by itself. This may be done even on Shabbos. [Gemara]

(24) "To improve them for eating." Even if the foods are already good as they are and he merely wishes to improve their flavor further, it is permitted.

(25) "Of wood." Although, as above, this involves both extinguishing and kindling, it is permitted because this is something equally desired by all people. Even poor people desire to improve the taste of their food, although such spices may not be readily available to them. Mustard in siman 510 is different because its preparation can ordinarily be done before Yom Tov. Know that some authorities hold that this permission applies only when the coals had already been kindled for food preparation, such as for a pot. According to them, one may not initially kindle wood solely in order to scatter aromatic spices beneath fruit over the coals.

(26) "And it is forbidden," etc., "upon garments." Even a garment that already has a fragrance may not have additional fragrance placed upon it in order to make it smell more strongly. Nevertheless, if an etrog had been resting on a garment before Yom Tov and was removed, it may be returned, because it does not thereby acquire any additional fragrance.

(27) "Because he creates," etc. This is rabbinically forbidden, because creating a new quality resembles performing a new melacha.

(28) "Fragrance." The same applies to placing an aromatic substance into water on Yom Tov in order to give the water a fragrance; this is forbidden.

"And even on Yom Tov following Shabbos." According to R' Ephraim this would be forbidden, lest the egg began being born today. We do not rule so, because the prohibition of hachanah applies only when an item's completion today results from preparation that occurred yesterday. While the egg remains in its mother's body it is not considered complete until it emerges into open existence.
